rows.stem: A student identifies a function from S to J as \(f = \{(S_1, J_1), (S_2, J_2), (S_3, J_2), (S_4, J_3)\}\) Check if it is bijective.
rows.context:
A school is organizing a debate competition with participants as speakers \(S = \{S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4\}\) and these are judged by judges \(J = \{J_1, J_2, J_3\}\). Each speaker can be assigned one judge. Let R be a relation from set S to J defined as \(R = \{(x, y) : \text{speaker } x \text{ is judged by judge } y,\ x \in S,\ y \in J\}\).
Based on the above, answer the following :
rows.solution: A function is bijective only when it is both one-one and onto, so it is enough to test the two properties in turn. Here \(f(S_2) = J_2\) and \(f(S_3) = J_2\), that is, the two distinct speakers \(S_2\) and \(S_3\) have been assigned the same judge \(J_2\). Two different elements of the domain therefore share an image, so \(f\) is not one-one. (It is in fact onto, since each of \(J_1\), \(J_2\) and \(J_3\) is the image of at least one speaker, but being onto by itself is not enough.) Because \(f\) fails to be one-one, \(f\) is not bijective.

rows.stem: How many one-one functions can be there from set S to set J ?
rows.context:
A school is organizing a debate competition with participants as speakers \(S = \{S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4\}\) and these are judged by judges \(J = \{J_1, J_2, J_3\}\). Each speaker can be assigned one judge. Let R be a relation from set S to J defined as \(R = \{(x, y) : \text{speaker } x \text{ is judged by judge } y,\ x \in S,\ y \in J\}\).
Based on the above, answer the following :
rows.solution: Here the domain has \(n(S) = 4\) elements and the codomain has \(n(J) = 3\) elements. A one-one function would have to send the four distinct speakers to four distinct judges, but only three judges are available, so by the pigeonhole principle at least two speakers must be assigned the same judge — which contradicts one-oneness. In general a one-one function from a set of \(m\) elements into a set of \(n\) elements exists only when \(m \le n\), and here \(n(S) > n(J)\). Hence no one-one function from \(S\) to \(J\) can exist, and the number of such functions is \(0\).

rows.stem: Another student considers a relation \(R_1 = \{(S_1, S_2), \{S_2, S_4)\}\) in set S. Write minimum ordered pairs to be included in \(R_1\) so that \(R_1\) is reflexive but not symmetric.
rows.context:
A school is organizing a debate competition with participants as speakers \(S = \{S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4\}\) and these are judged by judges \(J = \{J_1, J_2, J_3\}\). Each speaker can be assigned one judge. Let R be a relation from set S to J defined as \(R = \{(x, y) : \text{speaker } x \text{ is judged by judge } y,\ x \in S,\ y \in J\}\).
Based on the above, answer the following :
rows.solution: The given relation is \(R_1 = \{(S_1, S_2), (S_2, S_4)\}\) on the set \(S = \{S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4\}\). A relation on \(S\) is reflexive only if every element of \(S\) is related to itself, so all four pairs \((S_1, S_1)\), \((S_2, S_2)\), \((S_3, S_3)\) and \((S_4, S_4)\) must belong to \(R_1\). None of them is present at the moment, so all four have to be added, and no smaller collection will do — dropping any one of them would leave that speaker unrelated to himself. Adding exactly these gives \(R_1 = \{(S_1, S_1), (S_2, S_2), (S_3, S_3), (S_4, S_4), (S_1, S_2), (S_2, S_4)\}\), which is reflexive; and it is still not symmetric, because \((S_1, S_2)\) belongs to \(R_1\) while \((S_2, S_1)\) does not. Hence the minimum ordered pairs to be included are \((S_1, S_1)\), \((S_2, S_2)\), \((S_3, S_3)\) and \((S_4, S_4)\). [Note: the printed question paper types the second given pair with an opening brace instead of a round bracket. It is plainly the ordered pair \((S_2, S_4)\), and the marking scheme reads it that way; nothing in the answer turns on it.]

rows.stem: What is the probability that a randomly selected car is an electric car ?
rows.context:
Three persons viz. Amber, Bonzi and Comet are manufacturing cars which run on petrol and on battery as well. Their production share in the market is 60%, 30% and 10% respectively. Of their respective production capacities, 20%, 10% and 5% cars respectively are electric (or battery operated).
Based on the above, answer the following :
rows.figure: DECORATIVE — a black-and-white icon of a car with a charging plug. Purely illustrative; all three percentages the sub-parts need are in the passage. Not attached. Page idx 22.
rows.solution: Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be the events that the selected car was manufactured by Amber, Bonzi and Comet respectively, and let \(E\) be the event that the selected car is electric. The market shares give \(P(A) = \frac{60}{100}\), \(P(B) = \frac{30}{100}\) and \(P(C) = \frac{10}{100}\), while the production capacities give the conditional probabilities \(P(E \mid A) = \frac{20}{100}\), \(P(E \mid B) = \frac{10}{100}\) and \(P(E \mid C) = \frac{5}{100}\). Since \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) are mutually exclusive and together exhaust the market, the theorem of total probability applies: \(P(E) = P(A) \cdot P(E \mid A) + P(B) \cdot P(E \mid B) + P(C) \cdot P(E \mid C)\). Substituting, \(P(E) = \frac{60}{100} \times \frac{20}{100} + \frac{30}{100} \times \frac{10}{100} + \frac{10}{100} \times \frac{5}{100} = 0.12 + 0.03 + 0.005 = 0.155\). Hence the probability that a randomly selected car is electric is \(\frac{155}{1000}\), which in lowest terms is \(\frac{31}{200}\).

rows.stem: What is the probability that a randomly selected car is a petrol car ?
rows.context:
Three persons viz. Amber, Bonzi and Comet are manufacturing cars which run on petrol and on battery as well. Their production share in the market is 60%, 30% and 10% respectively. Of their respective production capacities, 20%, 10% and 5% cars respectively are electric (or battery operated).
Based on the above, answer the following :
rows.solution: Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be the events that the selected car was manufactured by Amber, Bonzi and Comet respectively, and now let \(E\) be the event that the selected car is a petrol car. As before \(P(A) = \frac{60}{100}\), \(P(B) = \frac{30}{100}\) and \(P(C) = \frac{10}{100}\). Each maker's cars run either on petrol or on battery, so the petrol fractions are the complements of the electric ones: \(P(E \mid A) = \frac{80}{100}\), \(P(E \mid B) = \frac{90}{100}\) and \(P(E \mid C) = \frac{95}{100}\). By the theorem of total probability, \(P(E) = \frac{60}{100} \times \frac{80}{100} + \frac{30}{100} \times \frac{90}{100} + \frac{10}{100} \times \frac{95}{100} = 0.48 + 0.27 + 0.095 = 0.845\). Hence the required probability is \(\frac{845}{1000}\), that is \(\frac{169}{200}\). As a check, this is exactly \(1 - \frac{31}{200}\), the complement of the probability that the car is electric.

rows.stem: A car is selected at random and is found to be electric. What is the probability that it was manufactured by Comet ?
rows.context:
Three persons viz. Amber, Bonzi and Comet are manufacturing cars which run on petrol and on battery as well. Their production share in the market is 60%, 30% and 10% respectively. Of their respective production capacities, 20%, 10% and 5% cars respectively are electric (or battery operated).
Based on the above, answer the following :
rows.solution: With \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and \(E\) as before, the car is known to be electric and we want the probability that Comet made it, so this is a Bayes' theorem calculation with \(P(E) = 0.155\) from the total-probability step. We have \(P(C \mid E) = \frac{P(C) \cdot P(E \mid C)}{P(E)} = \frac{\frac{10}{100} \times \frac{5}{100}}{0.155} = \frac{0.005}{0.155} = \frac{5}{155} = \frac{1}{31}\). Hence the probability that the electric car was manufactured by Comet is \(\frac{1}{31}\).

rows.stem: A car is selected at random and is found to be electric. What is the probability that it was manufactured by Amber or Bonzi ?
rows.context:
Three persons viz. Amber, Bonzi and Comet are manufacturing cars which run on petrol and on battery as well. Their production share in the market is 60%, 30% and 10% respectively. Of their respective production capacities, 20%, 10% and 5% cars respectively are electric (or battery operated).
Based on the above, answer the following :
rows.solution: Every car is made by exactly one of the three manufacturers, so once we are told the car is electric, the event "made by Amber or Bonzi" is the complement of the event "made by Comet" within the same conditioning. Using \(P(C \mid E) = \frac{1}{31}\) from the previous part, \(P(A \cup B \mid E) = 1 - P(C \mid E) = 1 - \frac{1}{31} = \frac{30}{31}\). Computing it directly gives the same value: \(P(A \mid E) = \frac{0.12}{0.155} = \frac{24}{31}\) and \(P(B \mid E) = \frac{0.03}{0.155} = \frac{6}{31}\), and since \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive, \(P(A \cup B \mid E) = \frac{24}{31} + \frac{6}{31} = \frac{30}{31}\).

rows.stem: Find the intervals on which the \(f(x)\) is increasing or decreasing, \(x \in [0, \pi]\).
rows.context:
A small town is analyzing the pattern of a new street light installation. The lights are set up in such a way that the intensity of light at any point \(x\) metres from the start of the street can be modelled by \(f(x) = e^x \sin x\), where \(x\) is in metres.
Based on the above, answer the following :
rows.figure: DECORATIVE — a night photograph of a lit street. It carries no data; the model f(x) = e^x sin x and the interval are given in the passage and the sub-parts. Not attached. Page idx 22. Note the photo is printed ABOVE the passage text on this question, unlike Q36 and Q37 where it sits below.
rows.solution: Here \(f(x) = e^x \sin x\), so by the product rule \(f'(x) = e^x \sin x + e^x \cos x = e^x(\sin x + \cos x)\). Since \(e^x > 0\) for every real \(x\), the sign of \(f'\) is decided entirely by \(\sin x + \cos x\), which can be written as \(\sqrt{2}\,\sin\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\). For a critical point we set \(f'(x) = 0\), giving \(\cos x = -\sin x\), i.e. \(\tan x = -1\), whose only solution in \((0, \pi)\) is \(x = \frac{3\pi}{4}\). Now for \(x \in \left[0, \frac{3\pi}{4}\right]\) we have \(x + \frac{\pi}{4} \in \left[\frac{\pi}{4}, \pi\right]\), where the sine is non-negative, so \(f'(x) \ge 0\); and for \(x \in \left[\frac{3\pi}{4}, \pi\right]\) we have \(x + \frac{\pi}{4} \in \left[\pi, \frac{5\pi}{4}\right]\), where the sine is non-positive, so \(f'(x) \le 0\). Hence \(f\) is increasing on \(\left[0, \frac{3\pi}{4}\right]\) and decreasing on \(\left[\frac{3\pi}{4}, \pi\right]\). The marking scheme adds that the open or half-open versions of these two intervals are equally acceptable, since the derivative vanishes only at the single point \(x = \frac{3\pi}{4}\).

rows.stem: Verify, whether each critical point when \(x \in [0, \pi]\) is a point of local maximum or local minimum or a point of inflexion.
rows.context:
A small town is analyzing the pattern of a new street light installation. The lights are set up in such a way that the intensity of light at any point \(x\) metres from the start of the street can be modelled by \(f(x) = e^x \sin x\), where \(x\) is in metres.
Based on the above, answer the following :
rows.solution: From part (i), \(f'(x) = e^x(\sin x + \cos x)\), and the only critical point in \([0, \pi]\) is \(x = \frac{3\pi}{4}\); the end points do not qualify, since \(f'(0) = 1\) and \(f'(\pi) = -e^{\pi}\) are both non-zero. Differentiating once more by the product rule, \(f''(x) = e^x(\sin x + \cos x) + e^x(\cos x - \sin x) = 2e^x \cos x\). Evaluating at the critical point, \(f''\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = 2e^{3\pi/4}\cos\frac{3\pi}{4} = 2e^{3\pi/4}\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = -\sqrt{2}\,e^{3\pi/4}\), which is negative. By the second derivative test, \(x = \frac{3\pi}{4}\) is therefore a point of local maximum. It is not a point of local minimum, and it is not a point of inflexion either, because an inflexion point would require \(f''\) to vanish and change sign there, whereas \(f''\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\) is non-zero. The local maximum value is \(f\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = e^{3\pi/4}\sin\frac{3\pi}{4} = \frac{e^{3\pi/4}}{\sqrt{2}}\).
